The Doughnut Economy of Port Anselm

When the last container crane left Port Anselm in the winter of 2019, the town council did something unusual: nothing. For eight months the harbour sat empty, the gulls reorganised themselves, and the only economic activity on the quay was a single van selling doughnuts to nobody in particular.

What happened next has become a case study in seven economics departments. The van became two vans. The two vans became a cooperative. The cooperative bought the crane.

The numbers are difficult to argue with. Annual doughnut throughput now exceeds the port's final year of container traffic, measured in units if not in tonnage. The council publishes the figures every quarter, in a table that has become a small local ritual.

YearDoughnuts (k)Containers
2019124,100
20229800
20252,3400

The cooperative's booking system, famously, is a shell script. It has not been modified since 2021, a fact the harbourmaster mentions with the same pride other towns reserve for cathedrals.

#\!/bin/sh
# port-anselm booking ledger
echo "$(date -Iseconds) $1 $2" >> /var/lib/anselm/ledger
sort -o /var/lib/anselm/ledger /var/lib/anselm/ledger

“We did not pivot. We just stopped pretending the sea owed us anything.” — Harbourmaster E. Voss

Economists who visit looking for a replicable model tend to leave with a paper bag and mild frustration. The model, residents insist, is the absence of one. The tide table on the cooperative's wall is the only KPI anyone will admit to tracking, and it is accurate to the minute.

Still, the lesson travels. Three other post-industrial harbours have started their own van-first regeneration schemes this year, each with a different pastry and identical scepticism from the regional development board.
